Fibres are raw materials used to make yarns and fabrics. Their characteristics influence the finished textile.
Natural and manufactured are the two main fibre classifications. The classification describes how fibres originate.
Plant fibres are commonly described as cellulose fibres. Their material source is plant-based.

Staple fibres are short lengths and filament fibres are continuous lengths. Fibre length changes how yarn is produced and behaves.
Spinning draws out fibres and adds twist. Twist binds fibres into a usable yarn structure.
Higher twist generally produces a stronger yarn. Tighter fibre binding improves cohesion.

Woven fabric interlaces warp and weft yarns. Two yarn systems cross to form the structure.
Warp runs along the fabric length and weft across its width. The directional yarn systems define woven structure.
Plain, twill and satin or sateen are basic weave structures. Changing the interlacing pattern changes fabric characteristics.
